title: The Obstacle Course — An Unfolding Story
synopsis: Two days before launch, a test fails. A tempting workaround competes with deeper design concerns, and your sponsor wants a decision by five.

opening.speaker: Omar Haddad
opening.title: The Failed Test
opening.text: The redesigned service fails a major customer test. Omar says to scrap the project; Grace sees a specific unresolved defect; Ben wants an immediate workaround.
opening.prompt: What is the first leadership move?

choices.text: Stabilize the team, separate facts from assumptions, and ask for a bounded failure analysis.
choices.reaction: Omar contributes to diagnosis, Grace's accessibility evidence is reviewed, and Ben can test a bounded option.
choices.coaching: Distinguish what failed from why it failed.

choices.text: Promise a workaround will save the deadline before testing it.
choices.reaction: The team sees a possible path but cannot yet defend its acceptance criteria or external message.
choices.coaching: A reassuring or incomplete answer may delay an uncomfortable issue, but does not remove responsibility.

choices.text: Blame the implementation specialist and order a launch regardless of the defect.
choices.reaction: An unverified shortcut becomes the plan and customers inherit the unresolved risk.
choices.coaching: Silencing evidence or substituting certainty for verification increases human and operational risk.

private-discussion.speaker: Omar Haddad
private-discussion.title: Facts Before Fault
private-discussion.text: Grace can isolate the failure, but Omar feels personally responsible. Ben argues there is no time for another review.
private-discussion.prompt: How will you separate root cause from blame?

choices.text: Require an accessibility check and acceptance criteria before approving Ben's workaround.

strained-trust.text: The team is exhausted and reluctant to question the launch date. Ben believes any delay will be read as failure.

critical-decision.setting: Service pilot lab · Decision and aftermath
critical-decision.speaker: Nadia Roberts
critical-decision.title: The Five O'Clock Brief
critical-decision.text: Nadia asks whether to launch, delay, or reduce scope. You have a preliminary cause analysis and two credible options, not complete certainty.
critical-decision.prompt: How will you frame the recommendation?

choices.text: Give Nadia a risk-based recommendation with options, confidence limits and a retest plan.
choices.reaction: Omar contributes to diagnosis, Grace's accessibility evidence is reviewed, and Ben can test a bounded option.
choices.coaching: Use bounded tests and risk criteria rather than false certainty.

coordinated-response.setting: Service pilot lab · Decision and aftermath
coordinated-response.speaker: Grace Kim
coordinated-response.title: A Controlled Recovery
coordinated-response.text: A reduced-scope pilot and explicit re-test would protect customer needs while preserving some momentum.
coordinated-response.prompt: What monitoring and exit conditions will you require?

choices.text: Document owners, communicate tradeoffs, and schedule evidence-based follow-up.

difficult-escalation.title: Sponsor Resistance
difficult-escalation.text: Nadia worries that a delay will be politically difficult. Your responsibility is to describe cost, risk and decision criteria without exaggeration.

fallout-recovery.setting: Service pilot lab · Decision and aftermath
fallout-recovery.speaker: Ben Wallace
fallout-recovery.title: The Shortcut Breaks
fallout-recovery.text: The workaround fails an additional edge case. The team realizes a full launch could expose customers to avoidable harm.
fallout-recovery.prompt: What will you stop, preserve and communicate now?

choices.text: Stop the preventable harm, acknowledge the failure, and set a transparent repair plan.

ending-strong.speaker: Narrator
ending-strong.title: Ending: Trust and Direction
ending-strong.text: The team makes a transparent, criteria-based decision. The controlled pilot preserves accessibility and produces useful learning.
ending-strong.reflection: Which observable behaviors made this result possible, and how will you repeat them?

ending-fragile.speaker: Narrator
ending-fragile.title: Ending: A Recoverable Gap
ending-fragile.text: The launch decision is partially stabilized, but tests, ownership and sponsor updates still require a stronger agreement.
ending-fragile.reflection: Which assumption or handoff would you revisit before the next decision?

ending-damaged.speaker: Narrator
ending-damaged.title: Ending: A Costly Leadership Pattern
ending-damaged.text: The team commits to an unsafe schedule. The unresolved defect spreads and a preventable failure damages trust.
ending-damaged.reflection: What would you acknowledge, repair and change first to prevent repetition?

injectChoices.text: Acknowledge the new development, confirm facts, assign ownership and adjust the plan openly.
injectChoices.reaction: The team gains a verified response and a shared next step.

injectChoices.text: Issue an immediate direction without checking the impact on existing commitments.
injectChoices.reaction: The new demand displaces work and creates confusion about responsibility.

injectChoices.text: Set the disruption aside and maintain the original plan without a risk review.
injectChoices.reaction: The unaddressed issue escalates while the team works from stale assumptions.
